faq: Do I need an existing iPhone app?
Yes. These targets extend an app you already have, sharing its data and design. If you do not have one yet, order an iOS app build and we plan these screens in from the start.
Can the Watch app work without the iPhone?
Many Watch apps rely on the iPhone for data, which is simplest and most reliable. Standalone Watch apps are possible for simple needs, and we explain the tradeoffs before building.
Will the iPad version just be a bigger iPhone layout?
No. We use sidebars, split views and wider grids where they help, so the iPad screen is used properly. Simple apps may only need modest changes, and we advise you honestly.
Which Apple devices do you test on?
We test on simulators for each size and on the real devices we have, then share a TestFlight build so you can check on yours. Tell us the oldest iOS version you must support.

desc:
iPad, Apple Watch and widget app development extends your iPhone app to the other screens your users carry. Ecom Swift LLC designs each one for its own size, from split-view iPad layouts to glanceable Watch screens and home screen widgets.

## What is iPad, Apple Watch and widget app development?

It is the work of adding new targets to an existing iOS project so the app runs well on more than one device. An iPad target adapts layouts to wide screens. A Watch target is a small companion app for the wrist. A widget is a compact view that lives on the home screen or lock screen and shows information without opening the app.

Each target shares data with the iPhone app but has its own interface, its own limits and its own way of being used.

## Why a stretched iPhone layout is not enough

An iPhone interface blown up to iPad size wastes the space. Text lines run too long, buttons sit far apart and the sidebar that people expect from iPad apps is missing. People also use iPads in landscape, in split view next to another app and with an attached keyboard.

The wrist is the opposite problem. A Watch screen is read in a second or two, usually while the person is busy. Anything that needs scrolling through a long form does not belong there. Widgets have a third rule: they show a small amount of fresh information, and tapping them should land on the right screen inside the app.

## How extra screens affect engagement

A widget puts your app in front of people each time they wake the phone, with no extra tap. A Watch complication can show the next appointment, a streak or a balance at a glance. An iPad layout makes the app comfortable for work that needs space, such as reading, editing or planning.

These surfaces tend to suit habits the app already supports. They help people come back to your app more easily, though how much they help depends on your product and your audience.

## What a well-made multi-device app includes

- iPad layouts with sidebars, split views and sensible use of landscape.
- Support for multitasking, such as Split View and Slide Over, where the app suits it.
- Home screen widgets in small and medium sizes.
- Lock screen widgets for the few facts people check most.
- A Watch app with a handful of simple screens and large tap targets.
- Complications that show one useful value on a watch face.
- Shared data between the iPhone app and each extra target.
- Dark mode and Dynamic Type checked on every new screen.
- Builds delivered through TestFlight on each device type.

## How we work

We start with your current app and ask which tasks people do most often. That tells us what belongs on a widget, what suits a watch and which screens benefit from an iPad layout. Then we add the targets in your Xcode project, build the screens in SwiftUI and connect them to the same data your iPhone app uses.

Basic adds one widget or an iPad layout for a few screens. Standard adds two targets, with widgets in two sizes and checks for dark mode and larger text. Premium can include a Watch app with complications, iPad layouts and lock screen widgets, with data sync with the iPhone app.

We test on the matching simulators and on real devices where we have them.

## Widgets and the Watch app, in practice

A widget does not run like a normal app. It shows a snapshot that the system refreshes on its own schedule, so we design it to show data that stays useful between refreshes. A Watch app has tight limits on screen size, memory and background time, so we keep each screen short and let the iPhone do the heavy work where possible.

## What to do, and what to avoid

**Do:**
- Pick the one or two facts people most want at a glance.
- Keep Watch screens to a single action each.
- Use your app's existing colors and icons on every device.
- Test widgets with empty and full data.
- Plan for people who have the app on iPhone only.

**Avoid:**
- Copying the full iPhone navigation onto a watch.
- Putting long text or small buttons on a widget.
- Showing private data on a lock screen without thought.
- Adding every feature to every device.
- Leaving iPad users with a layout that only works in portrait.

## Who this is for

This is for app owners with a working iPhone app who want to reach users on more devices. A fitness or habit app often benefits from a Watch screen. A reading, notes or planning app often benefits from an iPad layout. A delivery or booking app can use a widget that shows the next order or appointment.

## What we need from you

We need the iPhone app project, shared through a repository invitation, along with your design files if you have them. For TestFlight and device identifiers, we work in your Apple Developer account as a team member. We never need your passwords. A short note on your top three user tasks helps us decide what to build first.
